headings.title: Introduction to Anatomical Terminology and Body Regions
headings.content: Anatomical terminology forms the universal language of healthcare, allowing nurses across Nigeria and the world to communicate patient findings without confusion. The human body is divided into two primary divisions: the axial region and the appendicular region. Understanding these fundamental areas helps map out pain, lesions, and surgical sites accurately during physical examinations.

headings.title: Axial Region: Head, Neck, and Trunk
headings.content:
The axial region forms the main vertical axis of the body. It includes the head, neck, and trunk. 
- **Head**: Houses the cranial cavity and facial structures.
- **Neck**: Connects the head to the trunk, containing vital structures like the trachea and carotid vessels.
- **Trunk**: Divided further into the thorax, abdomen, and pelvis, protecting major cardiopulmonary and digestive organs.

headings.title: Appendicular Region: Upper and Lower Limbs
headings.content:
The appendicular region consists of all the limbs attached to the body's axis. These structures facilitate movement, grasping, and weight-bearing.
- **Upper Limbs**: Include the shoulder, arm, forearm, wrist, and hand.
- **Lower Limbs**: Include the hip, thigh, leg, ankle, and foot.

When documenting a client's injury, nurses must specify whether a finding belongs to the axial structure or an appendicular limb.

headings.title: Abdominopelvic Regions and Quadrants
headings.content:
To accurately pinpoint abdominal pain or pathology, healthcare providers divide the abdominopelvic area into four quadrants or nine smaller regions. 

| System | Divisions | Common Use |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Quadrants | RUQ, LUQ, RLQ, LLQ | Quick clinical assessments and pain localization |
| Regions | Hypochondriac, lumbar, iliac, etc. | Precise anatomical mapping |

For example, acute appendicitis typically presents with pain localized in the right lower quadrant (RLQ).

headings.title: Anterior and Posterior Surface Landmarks
headings.content: Surface landmarks serve as visible cues for underlying anatomical structures. Anterior landmarks include the sternum, umbilicus, and inguinal creases. Posterior landmarks feature the scapula, vertebral column, and gluteal cleft. Nurses use these surface markers to guide stethoscope placement during auscultation and to find injection sites safely.

headings.title: Clinical Applications in Nursing Assessment and Documentation
headings.content: Precise body region identification is vital for safe nursing practice. When charting wounds, rashes, or surgical incisions, vague descriptions like 'pain in the belly' lead to clinical errors. Instead, nurses document specific regions, such as 'a 2cm laceration on the right forearm' or 'tenderness in the epigastric region'. This clarity ensures continuity of care across different shift handovers.
